rubric.why: The law states that elemental properties recur periodically with atomic mass.
rubric.description: States that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete relationship; award 1 mark if only periodicity or atomic mass is mentioned correctly.

modelAnswer: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.

items.followUp: Define a covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed through electron transfer.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond as an attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: A correct ionic compound demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by the transfer of electrons.

items.followUp: Define crystalline solids and give an example.

accept: not arranged in a regular pattern
rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack the regular long-range arrangement characteristic of crystals.
rubric.description: States that the particles in an amorphous solid are not arranged in a regular pattern.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the absence of regular arrangement.

rubric.why: These are common examples of amorphous solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a true solution and a colloid.

rubric.why: Suspended particles settle on standing, unlike colloidal particles.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct settling distinction.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.description: Contrasts the suspension with a colloid, whose particles do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Suspension particles settle on standing, whereas colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle.
Suspension particles can be separated by ordinary filtration, whereas colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.

items.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give an example.

rubric.why: A weak electrolyte produces ions only partially in solution.
rubric.description: States that a weak electrolyte ionizes or dissociates only partially in solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: These substances are examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A weak electrolyte is a substance that ionizes only partially in aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Write two chemical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
rubric.description: States a valid reaction of metals with oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the property and its product.

rubric.why: Many metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
rubric.description: States a valid reaction of metals with dilute acids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the property and its products.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.

items.followUp: Write the chemical equation for magnesium reacting with oxygen, and name the product.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with hot water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen; the equation must be balanced.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with hot water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen; the equation must be balanced.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with steam.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

modelAnswer: With hot water: Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + H₂(g).
With steam: Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g).

items.followUp: Give four differences between an atom and a molecule.

rubric.description: States that a molecule has no net electrical charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct charge of a molecule.

rubric.why: A molecular ion carries a net positive or negative charge.
rubric.description: States that a molecular ion carries a net charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct charge of a molecular ion.

rubric.why: A neutral molecular formula is a valid example of a molecule.
rubric.description: Gives a valid molecule as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct molecule example.

rubric.why: A formula with an indicated charge is a valid example of a molecular ion.
rubric.description: Gives a valid molecular ion example with its charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct molecular ion example.

modelAnswer: A molecule is electrically neutral, whereas a molecular ion carries a net positive or negative charge.
A molecule is a group of atoms that exists as a neutral particle; a molecular ion is a group of covalently bonded atoms that acts as one charged ion.
The formula of a molecule is written without an ionic charge; a molecular ion’s formula shows its charge.
Examples: H₂O is a molecule; NH₄⁺ is a molecular ion.
